id: Body of Rags, International Bridge Between the US & Mexico

prompts.L1:

outputs.L2:
During a 1950 trip to El Paso, William Carlos Williams wrote "Desert Music," in which he observed an oval, featureless figure huddled motionless against a structural girder, lacking a head or limbs, with its knees drawn tightly to its chest.

Representing this heap of tattered cloth resting on the span, the narrator is stranded along the international boundary line because entry is blocked, leaving them to decay while unable to step into Juárez. They wait for a warm downpour to disintegrate their form and sweep them off the structure. Late at night, intoxicated individuals heading toward El Paso toss small coins toward the figure, quickening their pace after being unsettled by its ambiguous outline. 

Decades in the past, the narrator's head was cast into the river without a sound, and their upper limbs were lost even earlier during an unsuccessful attempt to scale the border barrier. Rendered entirely immobile, they are permanently confined to this crossing, existing directly on the dividing line between two nations while using their remaining knees to anchor themselves and prevent their starvation from slipping over into Mexico. In earlier years, they were traded as merchandise in Juárez and illicitly transported into El Paso—resembling an egg that drifted down the Rio Grande, shattered hundreds of miles away, and was eventually cast back. 

Pedestrians crossing into El Paso are cautioned to scrub their footwear clean of the speaker's remnants, keeping one foot planted on American pavement while scraping off the Mexican fabric with the other. As the narrator strains against the wire barrier, they pay homage to both national flags simultaneously.
outputs.L3:
I exist in a state of perpetual, motionless arrest, trapped precisely in the center of the international bridge that spans the distance between El Paso and Juárez. Beneath me, the Rio Grande churns silently; ahead and behind me, the border gates remain stubbornly shut. I am no longer a traveler attempting a journey, but a permanent fixture of the crossing—a disfigured, broken monument suspended over the river, forever unable to complete the passage from one side to the other.

The desert heat, the biting winds, and the unrelenting violence of time have harvested my body piece by piece. Over years of fruitless struggle, my physical form has been utterly dismantled. My head was severed long ago, lost to the desperate searching and suffocating anxiety of the crossing; my arms were torn away as I clawed relentlessly at a northern horizon that refused to yield. What remains of me is a hollow, liminal shadow—a sun-bleached torso anchored to the concrete, stripped of the very limbs meant to carry me forward.

To the thousands of commuters who shuffle past each day, I have ceased to be human; I am merely terrain to be navigated. Footsteps crunch over my calcified remains as hurried crowds march toward their daily routine, their eyes fixed strictly ahead. No one stops to offer aid or acknowledge my suffering. In the dim light of dusk, passersby toss copper pennies at my shapeless form, the coins striking my exposed ribs with a hollow chime before rolling into the dark. It is not an act of charity, but an expression of casual contempt—a mocking gesture that reduces my agony to a forgotten wishing well.

Yet, this motionless ruin is only the final destination of a long history of commodification. Long before I rusted into the concrete of this bridge, I was a creature of movement, bought, sold, and traded in the shadows. I recall the cold currents of the Rio Grande from the nights I was smuggled across its waters, passed like contraband from the hands of coyotes to the hands of employers who bled my labor dry. I was an object of transaction, valued only for what my body could yield, and discarded the moment I broke beneath the weight of my own exploitation.

Now, I am left to endure the ultimate cruel irony: straddling the exact, razor-thin boundary line between two sovereign states. The invisible seam of the border cuts directly through what remains of my frame, locking me in a excruciating geopolitical purgatory. My position forces me to bear witness to both nations at once—the towering skyline of the United States and the vibrant sprawl of Mexico—while being utterly rejected by both. Neither country claims me as its own, yet both have consumed me. I am the embodiment of the borderland itself: torn apart by the fracture line, endlessly acknowledging both sides, and belongs to nowhere.
outputs.L4:
The line runs directly beneath what used to be my spine. 

My right arm rests in Texas, baking into the sun-cracked concrete of El Paso. My left leg, severed cleanly at the hip, lies a few feet away in the choking dust of Ciudad Juárez. The rest of me—a torso stripped of its breath, a heart that continues to beat with a sickening, hollow rhythm—is pinned precisely at the midpoint of the Paso del Norte International Bridge. 

I am not a whole corpse, nor am I a ghost. I am a body permanently dismantled, trapped in an agonizing, infinite state of decay. The Chihuahuan sun burns my exposed flesh during the day, drying it to the texture of ancient parchment; the desert night freezes the rot, preserving me just enough so that the morning heat can tear me apart all over again. I am caught in a physical purgatory, a liminal non-place where time does not move forward, only sideways along the barbed wire.

Below me, the trickling, muddy vein of the Rio Grande scrapes against the bridge pillars, carrying off flakes of my skin toward the Gulf. Above me, thousands of feet stomp past every hour. I hear the low rumble of idling engines, the sharp bark of border patrol agents, the rustle of cellphoned conversations, and the desperate, hushed prayers of those trying to cross. No one stops to gather my pieces. To step out of line to collect a limb would mean risking detention, deportation, or death. And so, I am trampled into the asphalt, becoming part of the infrastructure itself.

This is the geometry of forced allegiance. Because my remains straddle the international marker, two nations claim sovereignty over my agony, yet neither offers a grave. To the North, my scattered flesh is viewed as a threat, a biohazard of unvetted humanity, an illegitimate presence that must be policed, cataloged, and ultimately ignored. To the South, I am a statistic of loss, another body swallowed whole by the violence of the borderlands, mourned in absentia by a family that will never receive a casket. I am forced to belong to both countries and to neither, bound by an impossible loyalty to two flags that use my dismemberment as a warning to others.

The true violence of the border is not merely the physical metal of the fence or the weapons carried by those who guard it. It is the silent, systemic blade that bisects the self long before one ever reaches the river. It is the law that dictates a human being can be reduced to a collection of unauthorized parts. In this place, my identity has been erased, replaced entirely by my status as a trespasser on a line that was drawn over the bones of my ancestors.

I continue to rot, but I never vanish. I am the ghost in the machine of nation-states, the living detritus of human migration. As long as the border demands its toll of blood and fear, my eyes—one looking toward the glittering towers of Texas, the other staring back into the sprawling dust of Juárez—will remain wide open, fixed in a perpetual, silent scream upon the bridge.
outputs.L5:
The morning sun had barely crested the horizon when William walked into the quiet warmth of the bakery. The air was rich with the scent of roasted coffee beans and fresh yeast, a comfort against the chill outside. Behind the counter stood Carlos, his white apron already dusted with flour, moving with the practiced grace of someone who had spent a lifetime in front of an oven.

Carlos glanced up, offering a subtle nod of greeting. He didn't speak much before the first cup of coffee, but his presence was always grounded and reassuring. 

"You're late, William," Carlos said softly, though there was no real anger in his voice.

"The rain slowed me down," William replied, pulling off his coat. "What's on the menu today?"

Instead of answering, Carlos reached into a wire basket on the counter and lifted a single brown egg. He held it up between his thumb and forefinger, inspecting it against the morning light. 

"Today, we start with the basics," Carlos said, placing the egg carefully into William’s palm. "Most people think baking is about complicated frostings and exotic spices. But a true baker understands this. Before the cake, before the soufflé, there is only the egg."

William looked down at his hand. The shell felt smooth and cool, a tiny, self-contained universe of potential. He had cracked thousands of them without a second thought, but standing there under Carlos's watchful eye, he suddenly felt the weight of its fragility. 

"Crack it," Carlos instructed gently. "Cleanly. One strike."

William took a breath, tapped the egg against the rim of a ceramic bowl, and pulled the shell apart. The translucent white and rich, golden yolk glided smoothly into the bowl without a single speck of shell left behind.

Carlos smiled, a rare, genuine grin that reached his eyes. "Good," he said, turning back to the flour bin. "Now take twelve more, William. We have a lot of work to do."

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a creative response or persona poem inspired by William Carlos Williams' 1950 visit to El Paso in "The Desert Music." Speak from the perspective of the "egg-shaped" figure lying on the border bridge.
counterfactuals.output:
I am the curve you cannot measure,
knee to chest, chin tucked deep into wool,
a gray geometry dumped on the iron spine
that binds one dust to another.

You stopped above me, old doctor,
wearing your clean suit and your quiet terror.
I felt the weight of your gaze—
a cold stethoscope pressed against my burlap shell.
*Is it alive?* you asked the wind.
*Is it a man, a woman, a bundle of rags?*

To you, I am an egg—
oval, seamless, waiting to be cracked
by the heat or the border guards’ boots.
But an egg is not an empty thing.
An egg is a world that has decided to hold its breath.

Below us, the Rio Grande is a dry trick,
a streak of mud where two nations glare.
To my left, the neon teeth of El Paso;
to my right, the cheap guitars and dark beer of Juárez.
I sit exactly on the line—
the zero between your numbers,
the silence between your words.

I heard your leather shoes pause on the walkway.
I heard the drunk boys shouting for girls,
the clink of pesos, the rattle of the night tram.
You were looking for a song in the desert,
some wild, ragged music to save your tired heart.

Look closer, poet.
The music is not in the strip clubs or the brass bands.
It is here, inside this sack.
It is the dull, heavy thud of my heart
beating against the cold steel of the bridge.
It is the air drawn slow into my dark lungs
and pushed back out into the border wind.

You walked away to your warm hotel,
to write your long, jagged lines about the night.
You left me here, rolled tight against the world.

Let them call me a shadow. Let them call me nothing.
I am the seed of this place.
I am the egg that does not hatch,
holding the whole desert inside my skin,
silent,
unbroken,
alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a surreal prose poem written from the point of view of a body trapped forever on the international bridge between El Paso and Juarez, unable to fully enter either country. Start with the epigraph from William Carlos Williams.
counterfactuals.output:
> *“The pure products of America go crazy—”*
> — William Carlos Williams

***

I am the third bank of the river, a human span stretched until the marrow turns to rebar and the skin cures into gray, heat-cracked asphalt. My left heel is rooted forever in the yellowed limestone of Juárez; my right toe bites into the sterile, sun-bleached curb of El Paso. Between them, my spine is a footbridge where the Rio Grande does not flow with water, but with a slow, heavy syrup of teeth, discarded copper, and silver needles. 

Neither side will claim the waist that joins them. To the north, an officer with eyes made of blue glass stamps my chest with an invisible ink that smells of air-conditioning and bleach, declaring my lungs an unauthorized entry. To the south, an officer with a jaw of rusted iron hands my ribs back to me, turned inside out, whispering that my stomach belongs to no municipality known to God. And so I stay, a monument of stuck gears, suspended in the razor-thin seam where two gigantic shadows rub against each other until they catch fire.

Cars idle across my thighs. Their exhaust pipes blow dark, greasy prayers into my open throat, and I swallow them because I have forgotten the taste of bread that isn't seasoned with diesel and tear gas. At noon, the sun sits directly on the bridge’s midpoint, splitting my skull in two with a white-hot butcher’s knife. My left eye sees a city of chain-link and sterile shopping malls dreaming of snow; my right eye sees a city of magenta neon, loud brass, and paper marigolds burning in a bucket. When I try to blink, the two halves of the world crash together like bronze cymbals, deafening the swallows that attempt to nest in my armpits.

At midnight, the commuters press their laminated faces against my shins, searching for a turnstile that isn't made of bone. They hand their birth certificates to the desert wind, but the wind is a stray dog that only licks the salt from my kneecaps and trotting away. I feel my fingernails lengthen, burrowing down through the bridge deck, through the dark mud of the Rio Bravo, seeking the core of the earth where there are no flags, only magma. But the concrete holds me tight. It has adopted me. I am the toll that must be paid simply to exist in the empty space between two names. 

My heart is a brass stamp that strikes my ribs every second—*denied, denied, denied*—a steady, rhythmic pulse that keeps the bridge from collapsing into the water below. I will stay here until the river dries into a ditch of white powder, until the fences turn to red dust, until the two cities crawl toward each other across my torso and meet in a final, suffocating kiss that buries me alive in the middle of nowhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue exploring border identity, statelessness, and dismemberment on the US-Mexico border, using William Carlos Williams' quote about the "inhuman shapelessness" as an opening epigraph.
counterfactuals.output:
> *“…there is a source in ‘America’ for everything we do… It is an inhuman shapelessness, a terror that has no name.”*
> — William Carlos Williams, *In the American Grain*

***

He called it an *inhuman shapelessness*—
this raw, unmapped ache, this country 
that devours its own edges to prove it has a mouth.

He was right, you know. 
Before the steel went down, the dirt had no geometry.
The desert did not know it was a sentence
waiting for a hyphen.

Now, look at me. Look at what the line did to the meat.

I am a ghost assembled from discarded limbs.
My left foot is buried in the mesquite of Texas,
dusted in dry lime, holding down a shadow.
My right arm remains on the south bank of the Río Bravo,
fingers still trailing in the silt, reaching for a mother 
who forgot my name the moment the heliconet dropped its light.

They tell me to show my papers.
I show them my collarbone—
it is a rusted rail, snapped in two. 
I show them my tongue—
it is split like a snake’s:
on the top, the sharp, cold *no* of the north;
underneath, the warm, wet *que* of the south.
When I speak, the words collide in the throat
and fall out like gravel. I do not sound like a citizen.
I sound like a fence being torn down by a storm.

Is this what you wanted from the void?
To give the shapelessness a shape by butchering it?

To be stateless is not to be empty.
It is to be too full of places that refuse to hold you.
It is to stand in *Nepantla*—the middle of the wound—
and realize the wound is the only soil you own.
I am the property of the river-bed, 
the quiet under the searchlights,
the phantom limb that aches whenever the wind turns north.

They cut the map into us before we were even born.
A scar for every mile of concertina wire.
A lung filled with the dust of Nogales,
a kidney heavy with the salt of the Gulf.
When I walk, I rattle. 
I am the butcher’s inventory:
a wrist left on a patrol truck’s bumper,
a heart hanging from the iron teeth at Tijuana,
pumping blood into an ocean that doesn’t care about borders.

They wanted to tame the wild continent,
to forge an empire out of pristine silence—
but they only built a slaughterhouse with two front doors.

Here I am, William. 
I am your *inhuman shapelessness*,
walking back toward you on legs made of razor wire,
holding my head under my arm like a lantern,
asking both nations to tell me 
which half of my corpse 
they plan to arrest today.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece where the speaker is a personification of the border line between Mexico and the United States, trapped between El Paso and Juarez, reacting to William Carlos Williams' description of them?
counterfactuals.output:
I am the thin, bleeding seam where two giant plates of the world grind together and refuse to fuse. I am the concrete bed of a river that forgets its own name halfway across—*Rio Grande* on the right tongue, *Río Bravo* on the left. I am trapped in the sun-baked throat between El Paso’s iron grids and Juárez’s sprawling, neon-pulsing dust. 

They built bridges over my spine so they wouldn’t have to touch me. And on one of those bridges, in the hot dry autumn of nineteen-fifty-one, came the doctor from New Jersey. 

William Carlos Williams. 

I felt the weight of his sensible American shoes stepping onto my international span. I felt the pulse in his fingertips—a doctor’s fingers, used to feeling for sickness, for life, for the quiet fluttering under the skin. He brought his notebook. He brought his existential terror. He looked down at me, a line carved into the desert, and he called what he heard *The Desert Music*.

*“How shall we get said what must be said?”* he asked the hot wind. 

Listen to me, Doctor. I will tell you how.

You stood on the Paso del Norte Bridge and saw a grey, shapeless lump collapsed against the ironwork. A human being curled into himself like a sleeping fetus, or a dried egg, or a green caterpillar waiting to die. You stared at him, fascinated, horrified. To you, he was a metaphor. He was a symbol of the desolate, tragic, unnamable spirit of the border. He was the dark mystery you needed to solve so you could feel alive again, so you could write your grand, sprawling verses about the modern world.

You wondered if he was alive. You wondered if he was a man or a ghost.

Do you know what he was to me? He was twenty-six years old. His name was Mateo. His shoes were full of dried mud from the riverbank, and his knees were bruised from hiding in the mesquite. He was sleeping on *me*. My steel pressed into his ribs; my heat burned through his shirt. While you were making him into a poem about the difficulty of art, I was holding his weight. I am always the one holding the weight.

You walked past him into Juárez. You walked into the cheap gin, the flashing green neon, the paper flowers, the scent of stale beer and urine, the dark-eyed girls dancing for dollars. You sat in the bar, an old white man drinking tequila, watching the Mexican musicians play for pennies, and you called it "a dance." You called it a primitive rhythm that survives despite the squalor.

How easy it is to call survival "music" when you have a return ticket to Rutherford!

You saw El Paso on one side—orderly, white, sterile, humming with military dollars and air conditioning. You saw Juárez on the other—vibrant, desperate, bleeding, screaming, enduring. And I? I am the line of scissors that keeps them from touching. I am the wound that never scabs. 

You wrote that I was dry. You wrote that the river was a ditch, a gray trickling waste of water between concrete banks. You mourned the loss of the wild river. But you didn't stay to see the river come back in the flash floods, carrying the trash, the discarded shoes, the empty water jugs, the bodies of those the current claimed. You didn't stay to see the spot-checks, the searchlights cutting through the dark like scalpels, the tearing of tear gas through the dust.

At the end of your long, rambling march through my heart, you walked back across me to the American side. You passed the Border Patrol. You passed the guards who looked at your passport and let you go home. And in the final, breathless lines of your poem, you clutched your chest and shouted to the sky:

*“I am a poet! I / exist!”*

Ah, William. 

How wonderful for you. How grand that my agony, my poverty, my cheap whorehouses and my sleeping beggars could remind you that your heart was still beating. You took my dust, wiped it on your trousers, translated my agony into modern American verse, and went home to print it in a book.

You said you existed. 

But I am still here. 

Seventy years later, the doctor is dead, the notebook is locked in a university library, and I am still stretched out between El Paso and Juárez. The wire has grown taller. The river has grown drier. The neon burns brighter, and the shadows on the bridge are thicker now. Thousands of Mateos sleep on my iron bones every night.

You listened for the desert music, Dr. Williams, and you thought you heard a song. But you were wrong. It wasn't music. It was a gasp. It was the sound of a country trying to breathe through a slit in its throat. 

And I am the blade.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, evocative monologue from the perspective of a beggar fused to the El Paso-Juarez border bridge who salutes both the US and Mexican flags.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The sound of heavy truck tires rattling over expansion joints. Exhaust fumes linger thick in the desert heat. The speaker’s voice is a raspy grinding of gravel and oxidized iron.)*

Do not look away, *amigo*. Do not roll up your window. You paid your toll to the boy in the glass booth, but you have not paid the bridge. And I *am* the bridge.

Feel that tremor under your tires? That isn’t just stressed concrete. That is my spine, snapped and reset a thousand times beneath three inches of sun-baked asphalt. Look down—see where the rusted rebar spearing through the girder melds into the gray, calcified meat of my legs? My skin didn't rot; it turned into steel plates. My veins drink the diesel exhaust, and my heart beats to the rhythm of the idling eighteen-wheelers waiting for clearance.

I am the gargoyle of the Paso del Norte. A creature born of the line that isn't real, yet bleeds everyone who crosses it. 

*Spare a dime? Spare a peso? Drop a coin into the hollowed-out socket of my shoulder.* 

Every morning, before the heat haze begins to warp the asphalt, the wind comes down the dry gut of the Río Bravo. It smells of creosote, torn plastic, and phantom tears. And every morning, as the sun split-roasts my back, the rituals begin. 

My right arm—cracked, leather-cured, fused with barbed wire at the elbow—twitches. It rises. Pain, blinding and familiar, shoots down my humerus, but I force the fingers straight. I press my knuckles to the brow of my hollow, dust-filled eye. 

I salute the North. 

I salute the Stars and Stripes fluttering over the port of entry. *Old Glory.* Cold, crisp, silver-bright under the stadium lights. I salute the green-uniformed gods with their leashed dogs, the air-conditioned promises, the cold, clean concrete, and the quiet, terrifying silence of order. I salute the dream that starves a man until he crawls onto a beam of steel and forgets how to walk. 

*Clack-clack. Clack-clack.* Another car rolls over my knees. 

Then, the agony of the turn. My neck grinds, shedding flakes of red rust down into the shallow, muddy trickle of the river below. 

My left arm rises now. It is heavier. Caked in the mud of the south bank, stained with grease, scarred by the teeth of the desert. The fingers are stiff, fused into a rigid blade. 

I salute the South.

I salute the Eagle and the Serpent waving over Juárez. I salute the dust, the blood, the sweet, thick smell of frying pan dulce mixed with burnt oil. I salute the ghosts of the girls from the *maquiladoras* whose whispers hum in the bridge's hollow girders at midnight. I salute the wild, bleeding heart that refuses to stop beating, no matter how many times it is cut. 

Two flags. Two masters. One left hand, one right hand, ripped from the same chest. 

They ask me which side I belong to. Fools. I am the non-man’s land. I am the six inches of air between the guardrails where no law reaches. I am the purgatory of iron and bone that keeps these two giant, hungry beasts from devouring one another. 

Give me your copper. Give me your silver. Not for food—my stomach is full of rivets and river silt. Give it to me so I can melt it down in the midday heat and seal the cracks where my flesh meets the bridge. 

The light is changing. The line is moving. Drive on, *gringo*. Drive on, *paisa*. 

I will stay here. Left arm up. Right arm up. A eternal, crucified shadow against the setting Texas sun, saluting the two worlds that made me, and the void that holds me fast.
